extracted.intended_audience: university mathematics faculty, course designers, and assessment committees (Quantitative Reasoning instructors)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and assessment practices for designing, delivering, and evaluating undergraduate Quantitative Reasoning / Contemporary Mathematics courses (course goals, content, pedagogy, assignments, and program-level assessment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Data-driven, technology-focused instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Course is data-driven with a strong emphasis on technology: every class meeting is held in a computer lab and students use computers to gather data, do mathematics, and explore trends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Excel and other software to introduce topics, gather and analyze real data, and project change over time; provide on-the-spot computing support (dedicated lab and in-class assistant). Note challenges: many incoming students have weak computer skills; computers/internet can be distracting and require classroom-management strategies (e.g., software to block internet when necessary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Course content coverage (key topics)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Quantitative Reasoning course should cover: introduction to descriptive statistics (measures of central tendency; distributions; constructing, reading and interpreting statistical graphs; linear regression), linear models (average/constant rate of change; linear functions), number sense (scientific notation; unit conversion; rules of exponents), and exponential models (growth/decay; half-life; doubling time; exponential functions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exponential modeling was chosen over probability to broaden experience of mathematical modeling; students should learn to distinguish linear vs exponential growth and make comparisons to deepen understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of real-world data and motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever possible, introduce new topics using a data set or a real-world motivation (e.g., population growth, news-article data).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weekly activities should include analyzing data from current news/internet sources, fitting models to real examples, comparing models, and using software tools for exploration; this grounds mathematical ideas and motivates student work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic writing and formal presentations
rubrics_metrics.description: Students write analytic summaries and present their findings to the class in formal presentations; they also write analyses of graphs and tables and produce graded analytic writing about data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because many instructors lack experience evaluating analytic writing in math, provide faculty workshops and discussion groups about evaluating and encouraging student writing; portfolios and instructor feedback should address written analytic skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborative and independent learning activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should work both independently and collaboratively on in-class assignments and out-of-class projects (group investigations, long-term projects, team presentations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Course design should include many in-class collaborative activities and group-based investigations; use in-class assistants to support students with technology and group work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific student proficiencies / learning outcomes (course-level)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should leave the course able to demonstrate knowledge of key topics; examples include constructing and interpreting a linear function using constant rate of change data and correctly analyzing a complex statistical graph and writing two quantitative conclusions from the graph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop common-final exam questions and other direct assessments targeted at these proficiencies to ensure learning outcomes are met across sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to address general education principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructors may vary syllabus and select texts, provided they address the five principles of general education and meet the stated course objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Course proposals require QR Assessment Committee approval; flexibility in texts/syllabus allowed only if general-education principles and objectives are addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program assessment components
rubrics_metrics.description: The assessment model includes faculty reflections, student evaluations (committee-designed web questionnaire), course syllabi and course web pages, portfolios of student work, a sample of final exams (with common questions), and other items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple data sources to evaluate course effectiveness and inform course design changes and instructor feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portfolio contents and use
rubrics_metrics.description: Portfolios of student work should include graded final exams, automathographies and end-of-semester reflections, samples of graded analytic writing about data, and graded homework assignments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect portfolios from new faculty and a random sample of experienced faculty; use portfolio review to give individual faculty feedback and to determine whether general education goals (analytic reading and writing, use of technology, mathematical content) are being addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common final exam questions and holistic rubric analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of common-final exam questions was developed to measure student performance on each major topic; faculty were asked to use these common questions as a subset of their finals, and the committee analyzes a sample of exams using a set of holistic rubrics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faculty may grade their finals and assign weights as they choose, but inclusion of common questions allows cross-section comparison; committee recommendations may follow from holistic rubric analysis (e.g., encourage more coverage of exponential functions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Student surveys for program feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Student surveys (administered online near semester end) collect demographic data and ask about specific student learning outcomes for the course; response rates are typically high (85%–90%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use survey results to modify course content and teaching emphasis (e.g., reduced time teaching Internet basics once student familiarity increased). Include open-ended responses to capture qualitative impressions (e.g., reflections on ‘reasoning’ aspect).

rubrics_metrics.name: VCU course goals for quantitative literacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Students will: (1) think logically about situations with quantitative components; (2) make use of mathematical, graphing, and computational skills in real situations; (3) independently read, study and understand new quantitative topics; (4) explain and describe quantitative topics orally and discuss with others; (5) explain quantitative ideas in written form; (6) improve number sense and become engaged with mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure course activities (writing, oral work, projects) to directly develop these capabilities; course should serve as answer to ‘why non-majors need mathematics’ and act as prerequisite for statistics where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classroom time allocation and pedagogical principle
rubrics_metrics.description: A guiding principle: approximately one third of class time should be devoted to directed instructional activities (lecture, skill review), and two thirds to active involvement (worksheets, group activities, projects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require students to communicate and write about quantitative issues (the best way to learn is to require communication); adopt cooperative learning and active-engagement pedagogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Student assignment and assessment requirements (VCU)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students are expected to: make weekly entries in a learning log responding to prompts; work as a team to deliver an oral presentation; write two three-page typed mathematics papers; undertake a small independent study project culminating in a poster presentation; participate in many collaborative in-class activities; complete four quizzes and three exams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independent study includes preliminary reports and a poster used to explain results; instructors should use provided rubrics to grade papers and presentations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment instrument design and topical coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment used a multiple-choice bank of sixteen questions covering topics: unit analysis, proportional reasoning, counting principles, interpretation of charts & graphs, general percents, percent increase or decrease, use of mathematical formulas, average, exponential growth, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions were piloted and revised; four different questions were included on each of four test versions; same four questions were used in post-test final-exam pages; interested readers can obtain complete question list from authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre/post assessment method and statistical significance threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the placement test as a pretest baseline and compare proportions of students answering topic-related questions correctly on placement test vs. on final exam; a significant improvement is declared when p < .05.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine question data by topic and conduct statistical comparison of proportions; be aware of placement test scoring rules and blank-response patterns (many students left items blank, affecting percentages).

rubrics_metrics.name: Piloting, sampling, and incentives in assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment questions were piloted with students and modified; four versions of the placement test were used and the same four-question sets were placed on finals; students were given one point extra credit on their final exam for each assessment question answered correctly (as incentive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design assessments with piloting and incentives to increase participation; sample finals for committee analysis and collect portfolios from targeted faculty groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructor support materials and grading rubrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide an extensive Instructor's Guide and supplemental materials including sections on in-class activities, learning logs, team oral presentations, poster sessions, student papers, and long-term activities; provide a variety of grading rubrics to help instructors inexperienced in grading papers and presentations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support a large contingent of part-time and graduate student instructors with clear guides and rubrics to maintain consistency and quality across many sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of teaching challenges and program limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge practical challenges: classroom sightlines are poor, daily computer use can be difficult, internet access is distracting, faculty need intensive training, budget cuts limit professional development, and the course struggles with identity (symbolic notation vs Excel use).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use in-class assistants, faculty training workshops, community of practice (cohort meetings, open-door observation), and ongoing faculty discussion to address these challenges and to refine course identity and pedagogy.
